end-pheochromocytoma.title: Pheochromocytoma
end-pheochromocytoma.summary: Episodic pounding headaches, sweating, and palpitations with a blood pressure of 196/108 mm Hg during a witnessed episode is the presentation that defines pheochromocytoma. sections.heading: Overview
paras: Pheochromocytoma describes the clinical picture of episodic pounding headaches, sweating, and palpitations produced by catecholamine hypersecretion from a chromaffin cell tumor. This entry is arranged in the order the problem tends to be encountered: what drives it, how it appears, how it is confirmed, and what is done first.

Reported frequency varies with the population studied and with the threshold chosen to define a case, so figures quoted in different sources are rarely directly comparable. The teaching point most often attached to this topic is that sequence is safety: unopposed beta blockade invites a hypertensive crisis.

sections.heading: Mechanism
paras: At the centre of the problem is catecholamine hypersecretion from a chromaffin cell tumor. Tracing the picture back to that single process explains why the individual findings travel together rather than appearing in isolation.

Compensatory responses mask the process early and fail late, which is why the interval between the first abnormality and the first symptom can be long. Understanding this is what makes alpha blockade before beta blockade and definitive surgery the rational first response rather than an arbitrary one.

paras: Patients most often describe episodic pounding headaches, sweating, and palpitations, and it is the tempo of that history — how quickly it arrived and whether it is progressing — that carries the diagnostic weight.

sections.heading: Examination
paras: Examination characteristically shows a blood pressure of 196/108 mm Hg during a witnessed episode, which is the finding with the greatest discriminating value in this setting.
A normal examination early in the course is common and does not argue meaningfully against the diagnosis.
